documents: Chaudhuri & Ghosh 2022, Geophysical Research Letters 49, e2022GL097962 (published PDF, 11 pages)

entry.evidence: Their activity offshore, however, remains elusive.

steps.action: Pose the question of whether slow-earthquake (VLFE) activity occurs offshore Cascadia. Known slow events are onshore, in the deeper transition zone, and the offshore trench is quiet in regular seismicity.
steps.quote: Their activity offshore, however, remains elusive.

steps.action: Take as background the published detections of VLFEs downdip of the locked zone in Cascadia and in other subduction zones.
steps.quote: VLFEs have been detected downdip of the locked zone in Cascadia

steps.action: Select Cascadia Initiative OBS broadband stations near the trench with quality continuous data, January to May 2014. The window is chosen to cover the early-2014 ETS event; the PNSN tremor catalog and the Stone et al. (2018) offshore earthquake catalog are added for comparison.
steps.quote: This study utilizes 3 component broadband data from the Cascadia Initiative (7-D) network of ocean bottom seismometers (OBS).

steps.action: Determine the horizontal-channel orientations of the free-fall OBSs from teleseismic Rayleigh-wave arrival angles (DLOPy), keeping only events with cross-correlation above 0.8. Remove the instrument response and band-pass the data at 0.02-0.05 Hz.
steps.quote: we use the Doran Laske Orientation Python (DLOPy) module

steps.action: Run a grid-search centroid moment tensor inversion over a 0.1° x 0.1° x 5 km grid with a laterally homogeneous velocity model, using 90 s windows stepped every 1 s. The best variance-reduction fit gives location, depth, mechanism and moment, detecting discrete VLFEs. The strategy follows Ghosh et al. (2015).
steps.quote: The study employs a grid search centroid moment tensor inversion method (CMTI).

steps.action: Use the CMTI-detected VLFEs as templates in SEC-C matched filtering of the continuous data. The threshold is the daily median plus 5 MAD. This yields 698 repeat detections across 12 families, and stacking the detections gives cleaner VLFE waveforms.
steps.quote: After we detect and locate distinct VLFE events using the CMTI method, we use them as template events.

steps.action: Run matched filtering on 100 random background-noise windows with each template's station configuration. This builds noise catalogs, checks that detections are not chance correlations, and sets the threshold.
steps.quote: We perform an extensive matched filtered analysis of background noise to inform the cross-correlation threshold

steps.action: Report 12 distinct offshore VLFEs (Mw 3.2-3.9) spanning about 550 km along strike and about 200 km along dip, recurring over the analysed months, with regional average depths and mechanisms (Figure 4).
steps.quote: We observe a total of 12 distinct VLFEs located offshore Cascadia as shown in Figure 4a.

steps.action: Compare the northern VLFE depths and mechanisms with the expected subduction-interface geometry. A 22 km depth is consistent with the plate interface, and VLFE 12 shows the expected low-angle thrust.
steps.quote: One of the nodal planes of VLFE 12 indicates a low angle thrust fault which is also expected.

steps.action: Attribute the mismatched normal-faulting mechanism of VLFE 11 to an unstable sub-horizontal nodal plane, low SNR and poor OBS azimuthal coverage, rather than revising the interpretation.
steps.quote: This is likely a result of a sub-horizontal nodal plane that can be a bit unsteady

steps.action: State the resolution of the estimates: horizontal locations are robust, but depth is poorly constrained by the sparse network and the CMTI method.
steps.quote: the resolution in depth is not well constrained due to the inherent limitations of the CMTI method

steps.action: Compare the VLFEs with three external data sets. Oregon strike-slip mechanisms match mapped USGS offshore faults. No obvious tremor accompanies the VLFEs. An Oregon cluster lies at the edge of a Stone et al. (2018) earthquake cluster, without temporal coherence.
steps.quote: A cluster of VLFEs occur right at the edge of a cluster of regular fast earthquakes in map view.

steps.action: Explain the Oregon strike-slip VLFEs from cited literature: aseismic slip in the Siletzia terrane, under-consolidated fluid-rich sediments raising pore pressure and widening the transition zone, oblique subduction, transpression and Gorda plate deformation. Infer that slow and fast earthquakes interact.
steps.quote: It is plausible that the VLFEs here play an important role in accommodating stress in this area.

steps.action: By analogy with well-instrumented Japanese VLFEs and the cited slow-slip origin of VLFEs, speculate that the poorly located Cascadia VLFEs lie near the plate interface and record slow slip.
steps.quote: we speculate that these VLFEs offshore Cascadia are also occurring near the plate interface and a result of slow slip.

steps.action: Keep the claim that widespread offshore VLFEs indicate a frictionally heterogeneous seismogenic zone hosting both slow and fast earthquakes, challenging the canonical homogeneous view.
steps.quote: Widespread activity of offshore VLFEs suggests a more heterogenous seismogenic zone capable of producing both slow and fast earthquakes

end.claim: Widespread discrete VLFEs occur offshore Cascadia (12 families, Mw 3.2-3.9), indicating a frictionally heterogeneous seismogenic zone that hosts slow earthquakes alongside regular ones.

decisive_move.sentence: The grid-search CMTI fit of synthetic to observed OBS waveforms detects and locates the discrete offshore VLFEs; without it there would be no templates, no matched-filter catalog and no claim.

gates.evidence: Action: no stated hypothesis directed acquisition. Data were chosen for proximity to the trench, data quality and coverage of the 2014 ETS (p. 2). Claim: detections faced a background-noise matched-filter test they could have failed (p. 4), but the heterogeneous-seismogenic-zone interpretation rests on consistency with cited studies, not on a test. Registration: the frequency band, 90 s window and median+5 MAD threshold rule were taken from prior studies (pp. 3-4), but the threshold was also informed by the noise tests, and no hypothesis was fixed in advance.

limits:
No peer-review file or earlier version was supplied, so there is no review sequence.

Composition is none_fits. The walk is question-led detection: data, inversion, matched-filter repetition, noise control, then interpretation by consistency with cited tectonic studies. No stated rivals share a crucial test, so it is not strong_inference or trace_series. It is not capability_first, because the question precedes the data, and the OBS network is existing community data.

Sub-claim statuses:
- VLFE horizontal locations and magnitudes: estimate_with_resolution, but the depth resolution is stated as poor and no uncertainties are given.
- Plate-interface slow-slip origin: speculative (the authors' word), resting only on analogy with Japan.
- Slow-fast earthquake interaction: a 'strong indication' from spatial adjacency alone; the authors report no temporal coherence.
- Moment-release significance: asserted, not quantified.

What the paper does not show about its own process:
- The noise test is reported qualitatively ('minimal false hits'), with no false-detection rate given.
- There is no independent data set or alternative detection method.
- There are no synthetic resolution tests.
- The text cites a Figure 5b that does not exist in the published figure, which has a single panel.
- The analysed span is given as January-May 2014 (5 months) in the main text but as 6 months in the Plain Language Summary.
- How the 12 templates were chosen from the CMTI output (variance-reduction cutoff) is not stated (inference).

disagreements.target: Canonical view of the Cascadia seismogenic zone as a frictionally homogeneous fault segment producing only regular fast earthquakes
disagreements.support: The paper rests this on the spatial distribution of the 12 offshore VLFE families near the trench and their adjacency to regular earthquake clusters and a slow-slip patch; no direct test of frictional properties is made.
disagreements.quote: It challenges a canonical view of a frictionally homogeneous seismogenic zone bounded by transition zones on both up- [...] .

disagreements.target: Prior accounting of stress release offshore Cascadia, based on sparse regular microseismicity
disagreements.support: The paper argues that the detected offshore VLFEs release stress not previously counted, but it gives no cumulative moment estimate.
disagreements.quote: a significant amount of stress is released by these slowly slipping events that are not taken into account so far

alternatives_considered.alternatives: gyro-based orientation as used for land seismometers
alternatives_considered.reason: orientation of free-fall OBSs is challenging and gyro orientation applies on land

alternatives_considered.alternatives: noise correlated with the template just by chance
alternatives_considered.reason: matched filtering of 100 background-noise windows gives minimal false hits at the 5 MAD threshold

alternatives_considered.chosen: Threshold of median plus 5 times MAD
alternatives_considered.alternatives: other threshold levels (implied by the stated trade-off with detection level)
alternatives_considered.reason: minimal false hits and a reasonable compromise with the level of detection

alternatives_considered.chosen: VLFE 11 normal mechanism treated as an artifact of an unstable sub-horizontal nodal plane, low SNR and poor azimuthal coverage
alternatives_considered.reason: sub-horizontal nodal plane can be unsteady, combined with low SNR and poor OBS coverage

alternatives_considered.chosen: VLFEs near the plate interface as a result of slow slip
alternatives_considered.alternatives: sources on faults within the oceanic crust or overriding plate (implied by poorly constrained depth and cited offshore faults)
alternatives_considered.reason: analogy with Japanese VLFEs located near the interface and the recognized slow-slip origin of VLFEs
